summary: Japan is a no-tipping culture. Good service is the baseline expectation, not a reward. Leaving money on a table or pressing cash into a staff member's hand is usually refused and can cause awkwardness.

rules.notes: Mid- and upper-tier restaurants add a 10% service charge (サービス料) to the bill; this is not a tip and is split into the restaurant's revenue.
Ramen shops, izakaya, conveyor-belt sushi, chains — pay at the front register, no table payment, no tip.
Drivers wear white gloves and often refuse rounded-up change. Large bills are fine.

Ryokan (traditional inn) is the one exception — some guests leave ¥1,000-¥3,000 in an envelope (心づけ, kokorozuke) for the personal attendant on arrival, inside a clean envelope. Modern hotels do not expect this.
Tipping a guide directly can feel transactional. A small gift from your home country or a genuine thank-you after a full-day private tour is appreciated.
Some high-end bars charge お通し (otoshi) — a small compulsory seating charge / amuse-bouche of ¥400-¥1,000 per person. It is not a tip.
Service charge is usually already included.
Uber Eats/Wolt drivers do not expect tips; the app lets you add one but it is rare.
